newsitem.title: UK: Forget nicotine-scientists coax blood from tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Forget nicotine-scientists coax blood from tobacco.

text.p: Scientists working in France reported on Wednesday they had coaxed human haemoglobin -- the molecule that makes blood red -- from genetically engineered tobacco plants.
The plants contain human DNA that instructs them to produce human haemoglobin, the researchers said in a letter to the science journal Nature.
They said their research opened up new possibilities for creating artificial blood free of infection from HIV, hepatitis or other viruses.

Michael Marden of the French research institute INSERM, who worked on the project, said the haemoglobin functioned properly when tested. "We have shown it does function," he said in a telephone interview.
The haemoglobin could be dissolved in saline solution and used as an emergency blood substitute, Marden said.

"One of the advantages of this type of blood substitute is that there is no cell," Marden added. "You don't have to do the blood-type matching because that is in the cells, meaning you could use it more quickly."
He added: "We are thinking for emergency uses (such as) automobile accidents."
It is nothing new to create plants that contain human genes, but this is the first time a plant has produced a complex molecule like haemoglobin, Marden said.
For instance, tobacco plants have been engineered to produce angiotensin-1 converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors), used to lower blood pressure.
The researchers employed well-established technology using the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefasciens to deliver the human DNA into the tobacco plant.
"That bacterium naturally transforms plants to its own end," explained Simon Santa Cruz, a plant virologist at the Scottish Crop Research Institute.
"It directs plants to make a sugar that only the bacteria can metabolise. Scientists exploit that to make the bacterium deliver human DNA instead."

Santa Cruz said although plants also carried viruses, there was no evidence they could be carried over into animals or humans. Therefore human molecules produced from plants would be safer than those produced by animals.

Marden's team, working with scientists at Biocem at the University of Cezeaux in Aubiere, found the tobacco haemoglobin, once extracted and purified, transported oxygen and carbon monoxide just like human haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin's role is to carry such gases in the blood. It gets its red colour when iron it contains reacts with oxygen.
"Although tobacco plants were used as a model system, other species may produce higher yields with simpler purification and sterilisation steps," the researchers wrote.
Currently companies produce haemoglobin for blood substitutes using donated blood that is out of date, and are working to get yeast that will grow haemoglobin.
Marden said he did not yet know how many tobacco plants it would take to provide a pint of reconstituted blood product.

More than half the current research on biotechnology is aimed at producing transgenic plants, such as plants that will resist weedkillers or pests. Transgenic plants can also be used to produce experimental vaccines.
